title: Master Tanluan's Pure Land Teaching
author: Compiled and annotated by Zhanran
excerpt: Single-mindedness means that thought follows thought without interruption, with no other thought intermingling.

inline.s: Single-mindedness means that thought follows thought without interruption, with no other thought intermingling.
With no other mind intermingling, thought follows thought
(in succession)
, even to ten thoughts; this is called the continuum of ten thoughts.
When at the end of life ten thoughts continue in unbroken succession, one attains rebirth.
Master Yinguang teaches

: Ever since Buddhism spread eastward into China, the First Patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Huiyuan, founded the White Lotus Society on Mount Lu; one raised the call and a hundred responded, and none failed to follow him, thus inaugurating the Pure Land school. Those who rendered great and conspicuous service to the Pure Land school: under the Northern Wei there was Master Tanluan, a man whose spiritual powers were unfathomable. On business he went south to have audience with Emperor Wu of Liang, and afterwards returned to the Northern Wei. Emperor Wu of Liang would often bow his head toward the north and say: 'Master Luan is a bodhisattva in the flesh.' Under the Chen and Sui there was Master Zhiyi, who founded the Tiantai teaching and guided beings to the Pure Land. Under the Tang there was Master Daochuo, who inherited Master Tanluan's teaching, devoted himself solely to the Pure Land practice, and in his lifetime lectured on the three Pure Land sutras nearly two hundred times. From Master Daochuo's school came a stream of outstanding talents: Master Shandao (the Second Patriarch of the Pure Land school), and then Master Chengyuan (the Third Patriarch), Master Fazhao (the Fourth Patriarch), Master Shaokang (the Fifth Patriarch), and Master Daxing, so that the lotus breeze of the Pure Land school blew far and wide at home and abroad.
Original text
"Yue
(a classical particle)
, from the time the great teaching flowed eastward,
(the First Patriarch of the Pure Land school, Master Huiyuan)

founded and spread the White Lotus Society on Mount Lu; one raised the call and a hundred responded, and none failed to follow. Those whose merit was great and manifest: under the Northern Wei there was Tanluan. Luan was a man unfathomable; on business he went to the Southern Dynasties and had audience with Emperor Wu of Liang, and later returned to the north. Emperor Wu would bow toward the north and say: 'Master Luan is a bodhisattva in the flesh.' Under the Chen and Sui there was Zhiyi. Under the Tang there was Daochuo, who followed Tanluan's teaching, devoted himself solely to the pure karma, and in his lifetime lectured on the three Pure Land sutras nearly two hundred times. From Chuo's school came Shandao
(the Second Patriarch of the Pure Land school)
, and on to Chengyuan
(the Third Patriarch)
, Fazhao
(the Fourth Patriarch)
, Shaokang
(the Fifth Patriarch)
, and Daxing, so that the lotus breeze spread everywhere at home and abroad."
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Letter to Elder Monk Ti'an of Daxingshan Temple)

[Master Zhiyi] Master Zhiyi wrote the Treatise on Ten Doubts about the Pure Land, and as its preface says: 'Works that praise and assist the teaching and contemplation of Amitabha pile up like mountains; only the Tiantai Master Zhiyi's Treatise on Ten Doubts about the Pure Land stands foremost of all. It cites the words of the sages and resolves the doubts of the multitude. In a room dark for ten thousand years, the sun comes and suddenly there is light to spare; on a water journey of a thousand li, once the boat is ready one need not labor under one's own power. Had he not been the later incarnation of Dharmakara (Amitabha Buddha in his causal stage, when he was the bhiksu Dharmakara), he could not have reached such a height.' [Master Daxing] Shi Daxing was a man of Qizhou. He entered Mount Tai to cultivate the Way, weaving grass into clothing and gathering fruit for food. Cultivating the Samadhi of the Lotus Sutra, he was graced with a vision of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra. Daxing sighed to himself: 'Human life is impermanent and must end in dissolution; who knows in what place the next life will be received?' Thereupon he entered the storehouse of the Buddhist canon and, drawing a sutra at random, obtained the sacred teaching of the Pure Land. He then devoted his mind to recollecting Amitabha Buddha for three times seven days (twenty-one days), when in the middle of the night he suddenly saw the lapis lazuli ground; the eye of his mind opened clearly, and he beheld the buddhas of the ten directions as images in a bright mirror. Later the emperor issued a decree inviting him into the inner palace; he slept in the imperial hall, was granted the title Bodhisattva of Constant Diligence, and was enfeoffed as Duke of the State of Kai. A year later he manifested a slight illness and passed away lying on his right side (the lion's posture). After burial, when the coffin was opened, his countenance was seen as if alive, and a rare fragrance filled the air. (See the Song Biographies of Eminent Monks.)
Single-mindedness

" is a fundamental concept in the scriptures, treatises, and practice of the Pure Land school, and a golden key for cultivation. In his Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, Master Tanluan, regarding the fundamental concept of "
single-mindedness
", clearly teaches:
Single-mindedness means that thought follows thought without interruption, with no other thought intermingling.
In the Treatise on Rebirth, Bodhisattva Vasubandhu says:
"World-Honored One, I
with one mind
, take refuge in and pay homage throughout the ten directions to the Tathagata of Unobstructed Light
(Amitabha Buddha)
, and vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss
(the Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Master Tanluan explains:
"The phrase 'I
with one mind
' is Bodhisattva Vasubandhu's word of self-admonition. It means recollecting the Tathagata of Unobstructed Light and vowing to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss,
with thought following thought without interruption, no other thought intermingling
(Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth)
[Tathagata of Unobstructed Light] One of the twelve alternate names of Amitabha Buddha.
Therefore, "
single-mindedness
" means precisely that thought follows thought without interruption, with no other thought intermingling.

Master Tanluan, Master Daochuo, and Master Shandao form a single unbroken lineage. Since Master Tanluan had already clearly explained the meaning of 'single-mindedness' in the Treatise on Rebirth, they had no need, in their later writings, to note everywhere that single-mindedness means thought following thought without interruption, with no other thought intermingling. This is something later students must especially heed when studying their treatises; otherwise, an error of a hairsbreadth leads one a thousand li astray. The claim of the Primal Vow teaching that 'Master Shandao's Pure Land thought is that the Primal Vow is not in vain and that invoking the Name brings certain rebirth' (see the book by Dharma Master Jingzong, Master Shandao's Pure Land Thought: The Primal Vow Is Not in Vain, Invoking the Name Brings Certain Rebirth) is one example.
Question: Master Shandao's Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles says:
single-minded exclusive recitation of
the name of Amitabha, one will certainly attain rebirth; let there be no doubt."
What is single-minded exclusive recitation?
Answer:
Single-minded exclusive recitation
" means invoking the name of Amitabha Buddha with undivided attention, unmixed with idle thoughts.
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu's Treatise on Rebirth says:
"The mind constantly makes the vow,
single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting
, and ultimately attains rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss; this is because one wishes to practice in accordance with reality
śamatha

(Translation: The mind constantly makes the vow and single-mindedly and exclusively recollects, so that at the end of life one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; this is because one practices śamatha (calm abiding) in accordance with reality.)
Śamatha is rendered in Chinese as 'calm abiding', the stilling of all idle thoughts.
Bodhisattva Vasubandhu's teaching proves that "
single-minded exclusive recitation
" means invoking the name of Amitabha Buddha with undivided attention, unmixed with idle thoughts.
In his
Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, Master Tanluan comments:
single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting Amitabha Tathagata
, and vowing to be born in that land
(the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
Thus, single-minded Buddha-recitation was taught by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu himself and advocated by Master Tanluan.

Moreover, in his Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles, Master Shandao calls single-minded exclusive recitation 'the karma of right concentration'. 'Right concentration' means right samadhi: body and mind pure and free from distraction. 'Karma' means the activity of body, speech, and mind.
This too proves that "
single-minded exclusive recitation
" means invoking the name of Amitabha Buddha with undivided attention, unmixed with idle thoughts.
In the Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra in Four Fascicles, Master Shandao says:
single-minded exclusive recitation of
the name of Amitabha, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, regardless of whether the time be long or short, never letting go of the thought
(the thought of Buddha-recitation continuing without interruption and not displaced by idle thoughts)
, this is called
the karma of right concentration
The original text is taken from A Brief Discussion of the Meaning of the Land of Peace and Bliss.
[Question: In the section on birth among the lowest grade it is said: 'When ten thoughts continue in unbroken succession, one attains rebirth.' What then is meant by the continuum of ten thoughts?]

Question: Concerning rebirth among the lowest grade, the scriptures and treatises say: '(At the end of life) when ten thoughts continue in unbroken succession, one attains rebirth.' What is the continuum of ten thoughts?

[Ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession, and one attains rebirth] When at the end of life ten thoughts continue in unbroken succession, one attains rebirth. The ancients, in writing, prized concision and loved four-character cadences, so that their sentences were neatly parallel and pleasant to read aloud. The 'ten thoughts' of 'rebirth through ten thoughts' means ten thoughts at the end of life; this was already common understanding at the time (and has been the common understanding of the Buddhist world for a thousand years, only to be thrown into confusion in the last dozen years by the inverted claims of the Primal Vow teaching). Hence 'ten thoughts at the end of life continuing in unbroken succession' was abbreviated to 'ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession' (and, read together with what follows, it plainly speaks of ten thoughts at the end of life continuing in unbroken succession). This kind of abbreviating rhetoric is found everywhere in classical writing. Unless one deliberately distorts it, no one could possibly interpret 'when ten thoughts continue in unbroken succession, one attains rebirth' to mean: if at ordinary times one has once had ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession, one attains rebirth.

[Answer: Suppose a man in a vast open place meets a hostile robber who draws his blade and comes at him fiercely, meaning to kill him. The man runs for his life and sees a river ahead; if he can cross the river, his head may be spared. At that moment he thinks only of the means of crossing: 'When I reach the riverbank, shall I cross with my clothes on, or take them off? If I keep my clothes on and wade in
(interchangeable graph)
, I fear I cannot make it across; if I strip them off and wade in, I fear there will be no time.' He has only this thought and no other concern; one thought of how to cross the river is one thought.
Such an undefiled mind is called the continuum of ten thoughts.

Answer: Suppose a man in a wilderness meets a hostile robber who draws his sword and rushes at him to kill him. The man flees for his life and sees a great river; if he can cross it, he can save his life. At that moment he thinks only of how best to cross: 'When I reach the bank, shall I swim across with my clothes and shoes on, or take them off? If I keep them on, I fear I cannot get across; if I take them off, I fear I shall not have time.' At such a time he has only the thought of crossing the river and no other thought, a single solitary thought: how to cross? Just this one thought. Such freedom from other mental attachments is called the continuum of ten thoughts.
[The practitioner is likewise: recollecting Amitabha Buddha as that man thought of crossing, passing through
(a variant of the graph meaning 'to pass through')

ten thoughts: whether recollecting the Buddha's name, the Buddha's physical marks, the Buddha's light, the Buddha's spiritual power, the Buddha's merits, the Buddha's wisdom, or the Buddha's original vow.
With no other mind intermingling, thought following thought in succession, even to ten thoughts, this is called the continuum of ten thoughts.

The practitioner is likewise: he recollects Amitabha Buddha single-mindedly, just as that man thought single-mindedly of crossing the river, passing through ten thoughts: whether recollecting the Buddha's name, the Buddha's physical marks, the Buddha's light, the Buddha's spiritual power, the Buddha's merits, the Buddha's wisdom, or the Buddha's original vow. With no other thought intermingling, thought following thought in succession, reaching ten thoughts, this is called the continuum of ten thoughts.
[Thought following thought in succession] Means successively, one after another.
The following passage was also quoted by Master Daochuo in his Collection of the Land of Peace and Bliss, which shows how vitally important it is.

[It is generally said: ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession. This seems not difficult. Yet the mind of an ordinary being is like a wild horse, and the consciousness is worse than a monkey, galloping through the six dusts without a moment's rest. One should, with utmost faith,
beforehand discipline one's thoughts, so that repeated practice becomes second nature,

and the roots of goodness become firm. As the Buddha told King Bimbisara: 'When a person accumulates good deeds, at death no evil thought arises, just as a tree leaning to the west must fall in the direction of its bend.' But when the knife-wind arrives and a hundred sufferings assail the body, if the habit has not been formed beforehand, how can the thought be managed?]

It has always been said that when at the end of life ten thoughts continue in unbroken succession, one attains rebirth. This looks as though it were not difficult. Yet the mind of every ordinary being is like a wild horse and its consciousness worse than a monkey, galloping through the six dusts (the dusts of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental objects); when has it ever rested? One should, with utmost sincere faith, train one's mind beforehand in single-pointedness and continuity of thought, so that repeated practice becomes second nature (through constant practice, making single-pointed, uninterrupted thought an instinct); only then will the roots of goodness be firm at the end of life. As the Buddha told King Bimbisara: 'If people constantly accumulate good deeds, then at the time of death no evil thought arises, just as when a tree falls it must fall in the direction toward which it already leans.' When the knife-wind of death arrives and a hundred sufferings press in, if one has never beforehand made uninterrupted thought second nature, can one at the moment of death achieve 'ten thoughts in unbroken succession' merely by wishing to?

[Consciousness worse than a monkey] The six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness) are more restless than a monkey leaping and bounding about. [Repeated practice becomes second nature] Through repeated practice, it becomes instinct. [Knife-wind] At the time of death a person suffers the agony of death as the four great elements disintegrate. Among these, the wind that dismembers the limbs and joints is like a knife, and is called the 'knife-wind'. The Sutra of the Recitation of the Correct Dharma says:
"At the sight of the end of life, the knife-winds all stir; skin, flesh, sinews, and bones, fat, marrow, essence, and blood are all cut apart."
The Sutra of the Five Kings says:
"When death approaches, the knife-wind dismembers the body, and there is no place that does not hurt."

[Again, it is well for three or five like-minded friends to make a compact together: when life is drawing to its end, they should in turn enlighten and remind one another, invoking the name of Amitabha Buddha on the dying person's behalf and vowing to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, voice following voice in succession, so as to complete the ten thoughts. It is like a wax seal pressed into clay: the seal is destroyed but the pattern is formed. When this life is cut off, that is the moment of birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss. Once one enters the host of definite assurance, what is there left to worry about!]

Therefore, it is best for everyone to invite a few like-minded friends and agree beforehand: at the time of death, they should in turn enlighten and remind the dying person, invoke the name of Amitabha Buddha for him, and encourage him to make firm his vow to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, voice following voice in succession, so as to accomplish the ten thoughts at the end of life continuing in unbroken succession. It is like pressing a wax seal into clay: though the seal is destroyed, the pattern is already formed. Thus the moment breathing stops is the moment of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Once one arrives in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, one at once enters the host of definite assurance; what then is there to worry about?

[The wax seal pressed into clay: the seal is destroyed but the pattern (the design) is formed] A wax seal carved with a design is pressed into a clay mold. When the mold is heated and dried and the wax seal melts, the design impressed on the clay mold is formed. The clay mold is the mold used for casting metal vessels. The Nirvana Sutra says:
"As when a wax seal is pressed into clay, the seal and the clay join, the seal perishes and the pattern is formed."

Here 'the seal is destroyed but the pattern is formed' is a metaphor for our cultivating with this physical body: when we have achieved the ten thoughts at the end of life continuing in unbroken succession, then at the moment breathing stops, though the physical body dies (the seal is destroyed), the great matter of rebirth is accomplished at the same time (the pattern is formed), for 'when this life is cut off, that is the moment of birth in the Land of Peace and Bliss'. [Why not prepare the thought beforehand?] Why not train beforehand in the unbroken continuum of ten thoughts? This is what Master Yongming meant by 'preparing the ford and bridge in advance'. Master Yongming teaches:

"If one's words and conduct do not match, if one's power of faith is slight and weak, if one has no mind of thought-following-thought in unbroken succession but rather the intention of repeatedly breaking off, and if one relies on this indolence, hoping at the end of life to be reborn, one will only be screened off by karmic obstacles, and I fear one will scarcely meet good friends; with wind and fire pressing hard, right mindfulness will not be achieved. Why so? What is now is the cause; the end of life is the effect. The cause must be real, and then the effect will not be false.
If one wishes to accomplish the ten thoughts at the end of life,
one need only prepare the ford and bridge in advance,
gather and accumulate merit, and dedicate it to that moment, so that not one thought is wanting; then there is nothing to worry about."

(from the Collection of the Convergence of Myriad Good Practices) [Accomplishing the ten thoughts at the end of life] Accomplishing the unbroken continuum of ten thoughts at the end of life. [Preparing the ford and bridge in advance] 'Ford and bridge' means a crossing place and a bridge; 'preparing the ford and bridge in advance' means making preparations beforehand.

blocks.text: When Ten Thoughts Accomplish the Karma

inline.s: Ten thoughts accomplish the karma: the ten thoughts at the end of life continuing in unbroken succession bring the pure karma (rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss) to accomplishment.

[The karma accomplished] The pure karma is accomplished. 'Pure karma' has two meanings: first, pure and wholesome karma; second, the undertaking of rebirth in the Pure Land. Here it means the latter, namely the undertaking of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. 'The karma accomplished' means that the undertaking of rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss has been accomplished.
In the Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, Master Tanluan teaches
"When one recollects Amitabha Buddha, whether by the general marks or by the particular marks, following whatever object of contemplation,
with the mind free of other thoughts and ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession,
this is called the ten thoughts
Simply invoking the name is likewise so.
He further teaches:
"The sutra's phrase 'ten thoughts' makes clear that the karma and the matter are brought to accomplishment
When the ten thoughts accomplish the karma,
it is merely that accumulated thoughts continue in unbroken succession and take no other object
(with no idle thoughts)
(Translation: what the sutra calls 'ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession' shows that the great matter of pure karma is accomplished.
That the ten thoughts accomplish the pure karma
is because thought follows thought in unbroken succession, with no idle thoughts.)
[The sutra says ten thoughts]
In the Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, the passage preceding "
the sutra says ten thoughts
" says:
"Following whatever object of contemplation, with the mind free of other thoughts,
ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession
, this is called the ten thoughts. Simply invoking the name is likewise so."
The karma and the matter brought to accomplishment
The great matter of the Way is accomplished. For the Pure Land school, this means the great matter of pure karma
(rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss)
is accomplished. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says:
"Furthermore, when a matter is brought to accomplishment, it is called the other shore."
[Accumulated thoughts continue in unbroken succession and take no other object] Thought follows thought in unbroken succession,
with no idle thoughts (
not fixing on any other object

blocks.text: The Difficult Path and the Easy Path

inline.s: The original text is taken from the Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth.

In the Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, Master Tanluan, following Bodhisattva Nagarjuna's classification of the teachings, divides the Mahayana teachings into the difficult path and the easy path: the Pure Land school is the easy path, and the other schools are the difficult path. On this, Master Yinguang says:

"The Great Collection Sutra says: 'In the Dharma-ending age, among billions who cultivate, scarcely one attains the Way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation can one cross over birth and death.' Know then that the one practice of Buddha-recitation is a path cultivated in common by sages above and ordinary beings below, a method that works alike for the foolish and the wise. It is easy to take up and lofty in its success; it uses little effort and brings results swiftly. Because it relies wholly on the Buddha's power, its benefit is surpassing and goes beyond the ordinary paths of the teachings. The ancients said: to study the Way by other gates is like an ant climbing a high mountain; to attain rebirth by Buddha-recitation is like a sail running before a fair wind."
(from the Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Letter to Ms. Xu Fuxian)
[Note: Bodhisattva Nagarjuna's Commentary on the Ten Bodhisattva Stages says: 'When a bodhisattva seeks avaivartika, there are two paths: first, the difficult path; second, the easy path.']

Bodhisattva Nagarjuna's Treatise on the Ten Bodhisattva Stages says: for a bodhisattva to attain the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika), there are two paths: 1. the difficult path; 2. the easy path.

[Note] A conventional phrase opening a citation of evidence or historical fact. [Treatise on the Ten Bodhisattva Stages] Seventeen fascicles in all. Composed by Bodhisattva Nagarjuna and translated by Kumarajiva of the Later Qin. Abbreviated as the Ten Stages Treatise, it is a commentary on the text of the Avatamsaka Sutra
Chapter on the Ten Grounds. [Vibhasa] Rendered in Chinese as 'extensive explanation'. [Avaivartika] Rendered in Chinese as 'non-retrogression': one's merit and roots of goodness no longer fall away.

[The difficult path: in an age of the five turbidities, when no Buddha is present, to seek avaivartika is difficult. These difficulties take many forms; to speak roughly of five or three, so as to indicate the meaning: first, non-Buddhist teachers appear virtuous and confound the bodhisattva dharma. Second, the self-benefit of the hearers (shravakas) obstructs great compassion. Third, scoundrels and evil men destroy others' surpassing virtues. Fourth, inverted wholesome results can ruin the pure life. Fifth, there is only one's own power, with no support from other power. Matters such as these meet the eye everywhere. It is like a land route: walking is painful.]

The difficult path means that in this evil age of the five turbidities, when no Buddha is present, to attain the stage of non-retrogression is extremely difficult. These difficulties take many forms; broadly speaking, there are the following five: first, drawing near to non-Buddhist teachers, which disrupts the bodhisattva dharma. Second, mistakenly cultivating the shravaka vehicle, benefiting oneself but not others, which obstructs great compassion. Third, scoundrels and evil men who destroy others' merit and roots of goodness. Fourth, inverted wholesome results, which ruin the pure life. Fifth, having only one's own power and no support from the power of another. Matters such as these meet the eye everywhere. It is like taking a land route, relying wholly on walking: it is hard and toilsome.

[The five turbidities] First, the turbidity of the age: the times meet with evil fortune and disasters arise repeatedly. Second, the turbidity of afflictions: people's minds are filled with greed, anger, and delusion. Third, the turbidity of beings: beings are of inferior capacity, with much suffering and little joy. Fourth, the turbidity of views: wrong views prevail and thought is confused. Fifth, the turbidity of life: beings, reaping the fruit of evil karma, are worn out in body and mind and their lifespans are short. [Five or three] A term for an approximate number, like saying 'three or five'. [The pure life (brahmacarya)] Pure conduct.

[The easy path: simply by the cause of faith in the Buddha, one vows to be born in the Pure Land. Riding the power of the Buddha's vow, one attains rebirth in that pure land. Sustained by the Buddha's power, one at once enters the Mahayana host of definite assurance. Definite assurance is none other than avaivartika. It is like a water route: sailing a boat is pleasant.]

The easy path means that one need only take faith in the Buddha as the cause and condition, and vow to be born in the Pure Land. Then, riding the power of the Buddha's vow, one attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Sustained by the Buddha's power, on arriving in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss one at once enters the Mahayana host of definite assurance. Definite assurance is non-retrogression (avaivartika). It is like taking a water route and sailing a boat: it is easy and joyful.

[The host of definite assurance] One of the three hosts. [The three hosts] The three classes of beings: the host of definite assurance, the host of wrong definiteness, and the host of indefiniteness. The host of definite assurance refers to those beings who will certainly realize enlightenment; the host of wrong definiteness refers to those beings who can never realize enlightenment; the host of indefiniteness refers to those beings between the two, who may or may not realize enlightenment.
[Question: Those who are born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, how many ranks and grades are there? How many causes and conditions are there?]
Question: For rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, how many ranks and how many grades are there in all? How many causes and conditions are there?

[Answer: In the Sutra of Immeasurable Life there are only three grades: upper, middle, and lower. In the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, each rank is again divided into upper, middle, and lower, making three times three, nine in all, which together form the nine ranks. Now, relying on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life for the praise, we shall discuss three grades according to that sutra.]

Answer: "In the Sutra of Immeasurable Life there are only three grades: upper, middle, and lower. In the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, each rank is again divided into upper, middle, and lower; three times three makes nine, which together form the nine ranks. Now, taking the Sutra of Immeasurable Life as our guide, we shall discuss three grades according to that sutra.

["The upper grade of birth has five causes and conditions: first, leaving household life and departing from desire to become a shramana. Second, arousing the unsurpassed bodhi-mind. Third, single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Fourth, cultivating all manner of merit. Fifth, vowing to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss. With these causes and conditions complete, at the time of death the Buddha of Immeasurable Life appears before that person together with a great assembly; he then follows the Buddha and is born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, transformed spontaneously in a seven-jeweled lotus. He dwells in non-retrogression, with keen wisdom and unimpeded spiritual powers.]

The upper grade of birth has five causes and conditions: first, leaving household life and departing from desire to become a shramana; second, arousing the unsurpassed bodhi-mind; third, single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting the Buddha of Immeasurable Life; fourth, cultivating all manner of merit; fifth, vowing to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss (the Land of Peace and Bliss). With these five causes and conditions complete, at the time of death Amitabha Buddha appears before that person together with a great assembly; he then follows the Buddha and is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, transformed spontaneously in a seven-jeweled lotus. He dwells in non-retrogression, with keen wisdom and unimpeded spiritual powers.

[Shramana] Rendered in Chinese as 'diligent and peaceful', that is, diligently cultivating the Buddha Way and stilling all afflictions; it is the general designation for those who leave household life to cultivate the Way. [Bodhi-mind] The mind that seeks perfect, equal, and true enlightenment, that is, Buddhahood. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says:
"When a bodhisattva first arouses the mind, he takes the unsurpassed Way as his object: 'I shall become a Buddha' — this is called the bodhi-mind."

[Perfect, equal, and true enlightenment] In Sanskrit, samyaksambodhi, rendered in Chinese as 'perfect, equal, and true enlightenment', that is, true and equal awakening. [Single-minded exclusive recitation] Always reciting the Buddha's name with one mind, without any divergent thoughts. (See
"What Is Single-Minded Exclusive Recitation?"
for details.)

["The middle grade of birth has seven causes and conditions: first, arousing the unsurpassed bodhi-mind. Second, single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Third, cultivating good to a greater or lesser degree and observing the precepts and fasting. Fourth, erecting stupas and images. Fifth, feeding shramanas. Sixth, hanging silk banners and lighting lamps, scattering flowers and burning incense. Seventh, dedicating this and vowing to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss. At the time of death the Buddha of Immeasurable Life manifests a transformed body whose radiance and physical marks are complete, just like the true Buddha, and appears before that person together with a great assembly; he then follows the transformed Buddha and is born in the Land of Peace and Bliss, dwells in non-retrogression, and his merit and wisdom are next to those of the upper grade.]

The middle grade of birth has seven causes and conditions: first, arousing the unsurpassed bodhi-mind; second, single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting Amitabha Buddha; third, cultivating good to a greater or lesser degree and observing the precepts and fasting; fourth, building stupas and Buddha images; fifth, feeding shramanas; sixth, hanging silk banners and lighting lamps, scattering flowers and burning incense; seventh, dedicating this and vowing to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. At the time of death Amitabha Buddha manifests a transformed body whose radiance and physical marks are like those of the true Buddha, and appears before that person together with a great assembly; he then follows the transformed Buddha and is born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, dwells in non-retrogression, and his merit and wisdom are next to those of the upper grade. [Hanging silk banners] Hanging colored silk banners in the Buddha hall. 'Zeng (
zēng
)' was the ancient general term for silk fabrics.

["The lower grade of birth has three causes and conditions: first, if one cannot perform various meritorious deeds, one should arouse the unsurpassed bodhi-mind. Second, single-mindedly and exclusively, even to ten thoughts, recollect the Buddha of Immeasurable Life. Third, with utmost sincerity vow to be born in the Land of Peace and Bliss. At the time of death one dreams of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life and likewise attains rebirth; one's merit and wisdom are next to those of the middle grade.]

The lower grade of birth has three causes and conditions: first, if one cannot perform various meritorious deeds, one should arouse the unsurpassed bodhi-mind; second, single-mindedly and exclusively recollecting the Buddha, even to ten thoughts continuing at the end of life, recollecting Amitabha Buddha; third, with utmost sincerity vowing to be born in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. At the time of death one dreams of Amitabha Buddha and likewise attains rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss; one's merit and wisdom are next to those of the middle grade.

[Even to ten thoughts] That is, even to ten thoughts continuing at the end of life. Master Tanluan gave a clear explanation of 'even to ten thoughts' in the eighteenth vow of the Sutra of Immeasurable Life: it means ten thoughts continuing at the end of life. In the Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, Master Tanluan teaches:
"With the mind free of other thoughts, ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession,
this is called the ten thoughts
When ten thoughts continue in unbroken succession, one attains rebirth."
"With no other mind intermingling, thought following thought in succession
(in succession)
, even to ten thoughts,
this is called the continuum of ten thoughts
Thereafter,
Master Daochuo likewise teaches in his Collection of the Land of Peace and Bliss:
"All beings
at the time of death
, when the knife-wind dismembers the body and the suffering of death presses in, give rise to great terror. Therefore, meeting a good friend (kalyanamitra) and arousing great courage,
with thought following thought in ten continuous thoughts
, this is a superior root of goodness,
and one attains rebirth
Moreover, as to the meaning of the eighteenth vow, Master Daochuo clearly teaches in the Collection of the Land of Peace and Bliss:
"If there are beings who, though they have committed evil all their lives,
at the time of death, with ten thoughts continuing in unbroken succession,
invoke my name, and if they are not born there, may I not attain perfect enlightenment."
The ancients, in writing, prized concision; hence when they used 'even to ten thoughts' it meant 'even to ten thoughts continuing at the end of life', without repeating the explanation.

[“Again, there is a kind that, though reborn in the Land of Bliss, does not fall within the three grades: namely, those who, with a mind of doubt, cultivate various meritorious deeds and aspire to be reborn in the Land of Bliss. They do not comprehend the Buddha-wisdom, the wisdom of the inconceivable, the wisdom of the immeasurable, the vast wisdom of the Great Vehicle, the unsurpassed, unrivalled, supreme wisdom; and regarding these wisdoms they are full of doubt and do not believe. Yet they still believe in offenses and blessings, cultivate the roots of goodness, and are reborn in the Land of Bliss. Reborn there in the seven-jeweled palaces, some a hundred yojanas in extent, some five hundred yojanas in extent, each within them enjoys various happinesses, like the Trayastrimsa heaven, all also spontaneously present. For five hundred years they constantly do not see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, do not see the bodhisattvas and the sravaka holy assemblies. In the Land of Bliss this is called the border region, and is also called womb-born.]

Again there is a kind that, though reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, does not fall within the three grades. This is because these beings, with a mind of doubt, cultivate various meritorious deeds and aspire to be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. But they do not comprehend the Buddha-wisdom, the wisdom of the inconceivable, the wisdom of the immeasurable, the vast wisdom of the Great Vehicle, the unsurpassed, unrivalled, supreme wisdom; and regarding these wisdoms they are full of doubt and do not believe. Yet they still believe in offenses and blessings, cultivate the roots of goodness, and seek rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. At the end of life they are born in the seven-jeweled palaces of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, the palaces being a hundred yojanas or five hundred yojanas in extent. Each within them enjoys various happinesses, like the Trayastrimsa heaven, with clothing, food, and drink all spontaneously present. For five hundred years they cannot see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, do not see the bodhisattvas and the sravaka holy assemblies. In the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss this is called the border region, and is also called womb-born.
[Yojana]A unit of distance in India. There are three sizes: a great yojana is about eighty li; a middle yojana about sixty li; a small yojana about forty li.

[“As for the border region, it means that during those five hundred years they do not see or hear the Triple Gem, the meaning being the same as the difficulty of the border region; it is also because those palaces lie at the very edge of the Land of Bliss. As for womb-born, it is like the first moment of a womb-born human being, when the human form and its faculties are not yet complete. ‘Border’ speaks of the difficulty, ‘womb’ speaks of the darkness
(same as ‘dark’)

. These two names are both borrowed to illustrate, and do not refer to the border region among the eight difficulties, nor to the womb-born of a womb. How do we know? Because the Land of Bliss is wholly birth by transformation, so we know it is not truly womb-born; and because after five hundred years they again see and hear the Triple Gem, we know it is not the border region among the eight difficulties.”]

The so-called border region means that the beings reborn in those palaces, in the course of five hundred years, cannot see or hear the Triple Gem; this is the same as the obstacle of beings in a border land who cannot see or hear the Dharma; it is also because those palaces lie at the very edge of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. The so-called womb-born is like a womb-born human being in the first moment of birth, before the human person is fully grown. ‘Border’ speaks of the difficulty, ‘womb’ speaks of the darkness. These two names are both borrowings to illustrate; it is not truly the border region among the eight difficulties, nor truly the womb-born of a womb. How do we know? Because the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is wholly birth by transformation, therefore it is not truly womb-born; and because after five hundred years they again see and hear the Triple Gem, we know it is not the border region among the eight difficulties.”

[Triple Gem]The Buddha-gem, the Dharma-gem, and the Sangha-gem. [Eight difficulties]Eight places and circumstances in which one is hindered from seeing and hearing the Buddha-Dharma, namely: the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, the Uttarakuru continent, the heaven of no-thought, the blind, deaf, and mute, worldly intelligence and eloquence, and the times before and after a Buddha's appearance. The border region refers to the Uttarakuru continent, whose people are prosperous and happy, with a life-span of a thousand years, yet they cannot see or hear the Dharma, so they cannot end birth and death.
The original text is recorded from the Record of Sages and Saints of the Pure Land.
Tanluan. A man of Yanmen in Shanxi, who in his youth traveled to Mount Wutai and there saw many miraculous and wondrous events, and so roused faith

and shaved his head to leave the home life. While reading the Great Collection Sutra, because the words and meaning of the scripture were profound and subtle, he resolved to write a commentary on it. He had written only halfway through his commentary when he was stricken with an illness of the breath, and so traveled everywhere seeking a cure. Afterwards he sighed and said: “Human life is fragile and precarious, subject to change from dawn to dusk. I have heard that the long-lived immortals often appear in the world. If I could obtain the art of the long-lived immortals, and then spread Buddhism, would that not also be good?” Therefore he went to the hermitage of the Daoist Tao Hongjing in the south of the Yangtze and earnestly sought the art of the immortals. Tao Hongjing gave him the ten volumes of the Scripture of Immortals, and Tanluan returned with great joy.

On the way back, passing through Luoyang, he met the Tripitaka master Bodhiruci. Tanluan asked him: “Is there in the Buddha-Dharma also a method of long life and deathlessness that surpasses this Scripture of Immortals?” Bodhiruci said: “In this eastern land of ours, where is there any method of long life and deathlessness? Even if you attain long life and for a short time do not die, in the end you return to the turning of the six destinies — what is there to treasure? True long life and deathlessness exist only in the Buddha-Dharma

Therefore Bodhiruci taught Tanluan the Sixteen Contemplations Sutra (the Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Measureless Life). And he told him: “If you study this sutra, you will not again be born in the three realms, nor again go to the turning of the six destinies; the waxing and waning of fullness and emptiness, fortune and misfortune, success and failure — none will again come to disturb or harm us. And its life-span is as long as the sands of the Ganges across kalpas, measureless and boundless — truly there is no way to measure or compare it. This is the long-life wonder of my Buddha, the great enlightened Golden Immortal.” When Tanluan heard this his heart was greatly delighted, so he burned the Scripture of Immortals and devoted himself solely to the contemplative practice of the Pure Land. Not only did he cultivate himself, he also taught and transformed living beings, and his virtuous reputation spread far and wide, its influence enduring and vast.

He once composed twelve verses of praise and worship, seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, to continue the verses made by Nagarjuna Bodhisattva; he also wrote a two-volume Commentary on the Treatise on Rebirth, which circulated in the world.

The ruler of the Wei dynasty greatly respected and honored him, and so bestowed on him the title of ‘Divine Tanluan’ and issued an edict inviting him to reside at the Great Temple of Bingzhou in Shanxi. In his later years he moved to Xuanzhong Temple in Fenzhou. In the fourth year of Xinghe of Emperor Xiaojing of the Eastern Wei (in the year

), one night in his chamber he saw an Indian monk, who told him: “I am Nagarjuna, long ago reborn and dwelling in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Because your aspiration accords with mine, I have come especially to meet with you.” Tanluan knew that the time of his rebirth had come, so he gathered the assembly and admonished them, saying: “You have all toiled and hurried through life after life, with no end in sight. The many sufferings of the hells must not be but guarded against; the pure karma of the nine grades must not but be cultivated.” Having said this, he commanded his disciples to recite the Buddha's name aloud, while he himself faced west, prostrated, and passed into rebirth.

At the time, all the people in the temple saw banners, flowers, and canopies coming from the west, and celestial music filled the whole sky, and it was a long time before it disappeared. These auspicious signs of response spread to the court, and so the emperor issued an edict to bury Master Tanluan in Wengu in Fenxi (present-day Pingyang, Shanxi), and there had a pagoda-temple and a commemorative stele built for him.
Recorded from the Record of Sages and Saints of the Pure Land.

Tanluan of Wei, known as Tanluan. A man of Yanmen. In his youth he traveled to Mount Wutai and saw miraculous and wondrous events, and so roused faith and left the home life. While reading the Great Collection Sutra, because the meaning of its words was deep and dense, he wrote a commentary on it. When the writing was more than half finished, he was stricken with an illness of the breath, and went about everywhere seeking medical help. Afterwards he sighed and said: ‘Human life is fragile and precarious, subject to change from dawn to dusk. I have heard that the long-lived immortals often appear. If I may obtain this method and then honor Buddhism, would that not be good too?’

Thereupon he went to the place of the hermit Tao in the south, and earnestly sought the art of the immortals. The hermit gave him the ten volumes of the Scripture of Immortals, and he returned delighted. When he reached Luoyang, he met the Tripitaka master Bodhiruci. Tanluan asked him: ‘Is there perhaps in the Buddha-Dharma a method of long life and deathlessness that surpasses this Scripture of Immortals?’ Bodhiruci said: ‘In this land where is there any method of long life and deathlessness? Even if you attain long life and for a short time do not die, in the end you return to transmigration — what is there to treasure? Now long life and deathlessness belong to the Buddha-Dharma of mine.’ Thereupon he gave him the Sixteen Contemplations Sutra, saying: ‘If you study this, then you will not again be born in the three realms, nor again go to the six destinies; the waxing and waning of fullness and emptiness, fortune and misfortune, success and failure, will not come to reach you. As for its life-span, it is like the sands of the Ganges across kalpas, and nothing can compare to it — this is the long life of my Golden Immortal.’ Tanluan was greatly delighted, so he burned the Scripture of Immortals and devoted himself solely to the pure contemplations. Practicing himself and transforming others, it spread ever more widely. He composed the twelve verses of praise for the Pure Land, continuing the verses of Nagarjuna. He also wrote the two-volume Treatise on the Land of Peace, which was handed down in the world.

The ruler of Wei honored him greatly, naming him Divine Tanluan, and commanded him to reside at the Great Temple of Bingzhou. In his later years he moved to Xuanzhong Temple in Fenzhou. In the fourth year of Xinghe, one evening, in his chamber he saw an Indian monk who said to him: ‘I am Nagarjuna, long dwelling in the Pure Land. Because your aspiration is the same as mine, I have come to see you.’ Tanluan knew that his time had come, and gathering the assembly he exhorted them, saying: ‘Toiling and hurrying through life, there is no day when it stops. The many sufferings of the hells must not but be feared. The pure karma of the nine grades must not but be cultivated.’ Thereupon he had his disciples loudly chant the Buddha's name, and facing west, he bowed his head to the ground and passed away. All those in the temple saw banners, flowers, and canopies coming from the west. Celestial music filled the sky, and it was a long while before it ceased. The matter was reported to the court, and an edict ordered him buried in Wengu in Fenxi, and a pagoda erected and a stele set up.
